subject: Live encounters and dead recoveries and model selection

messages.author: 843912d36041ca16
messages.subject: Live encounters and dead recoveries and model selection
parts:
Hi folks,

I am trying to estimate weekly survival probabilities for young shorebirds over 6 occasions ranging from the last week of incubation to the fifth week of life after hatching using information from live encounters and dead recoveries. I am trying a slightly different approach than the Burnham model outlined in the BPA book, but similar idea.

I have formatted encounter histories using an age-based time structure – rather than a calendar-based time structure – to focus on the processes shaping survival of young from hatching to fledging. Occasions are defined in 7 d increments relative to the hatch date of each individual. All individuals enter the analysis on occasion 1, as eggs in their last week of incubation. Subsequent encounters with individual young are detailed for occasions 2 to 6, the first to fifth weeks of life after hatching.

Three states are defined in the model: 1) alive, 2) recently dead, and 3) dead (absorbing). There are three types of encounters: 1) live detections, 2) dead recoveries, and 3) non-detections.

I am getting hung up on a couple of things. In addition to being interested in several fixed effects (including hatch date), I am exploring two different random effects on survival, detection, and recovery parameters: siteyear effects and brood effects. There are many models to consider that seem like reasonable hypotheses. 

Nimble appears to generate WAIC values fine but in some cases a "better" model according to WAIC shows poor mixing of chains for some parameters. Should I be prioritizing WAIC or mixing of chains and convergence of estimates? Or should I be thinking about different parameterizations? Or a totally different way to model these data? Or...?

Many thanks,

Justin

messages.author: 6ad895aa93bfdc63
messages.subject: Re: Live encounters and dead recoveries and model selection
parts:
Hi Justin,

I'll take a shot. Note, just one person's opinion.
  • If I were trying to select a model that has the best (leave-one-out) cross-validation properties, I might use WAIC. If interested in coverage of the 95% CI's (and not too worried about prediction uncertainty), I might just fit one "full model" with all of the pre-specified effects.
  • If a model was not converging or mixing well, I wouldn't trust/report the WAIC score. It's possible that nimble is throwing warnings about point-wise pWAIC>0.4 or whatever--if so, I would similarly not trust the score. Tactically, if a more complex model were scoring much better and the posterior indicates support for the random effects or whatever other added bells/whistles (e.g., sd's >>0) , I might focus on tinkering around to help convergence/mixing of this model. This might include swapping samplers, blocking certain terms, marginalizing over the the discrete latent states (e.g., nimbleEcology's dHMM family of distributions), etc. Tough to say what to do here. I might also check priors/employ a prior predictive check to make sure certain things are sensible. Just as an example, inv.logit(N(0, sd=5)) is bimodal, which may or may not be reasonable; the exponential distribution has a long-right tail, and something like a half normal might be better behaved.
  • Where this gets tricky is in the WAIC calculations, where there is some hand-wringing about conditioning on vs. marginalizing over random effects and where default calculations may not be what you want. Random effects here include the varied sds, and also the z's. I think nimbleMCMC uses the fully conditional WAIC. I think this implies that the score/penalty parts of the IC are derived from log([y_{i,t}|z_{i,t}*po_{i,t}]), which is a little like scoring the model based on how well the detection model (alone) fits. Using dHMM to marginalize over z, the model will be scored using log([y_{i,}|ps_{i,},po_{i, ]), which includes the contributions of the state model to the data likelihood. I think others are working on alternative approaches that would also capture the contributions of the state model. 
  • With the brood and site-year random effects, nimble provides some ways to control whether you want to marginalize over these effects and how you want to group data if you do. These are dense topics, and the links below and related are better references--it seems this has some connection to whether the comparison is predicated on leaving one individual out vs. leaving one brood or site-year out. 

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-017-9736-8
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31297664/
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.13359.pdf

John

messages.author: 843912d36041ca16
messages.subject: Re: Live encounters and dead recoveries and model selection
parts:
Hi John,

Thank you for offering your thoughts and links to references. I will confess that I am not excited to hear that some of the references cover "dense topics"!

A couple of notes that may be of general interest: I did try using a couple of different distributions for the standard deviations of the random brood effects. Constraining those SDs with a uniform distribution dunif(0,3) did enable better convergence of parameter estimates...but I'm pretty sure it also resulted in underestimates of the true heterogeneity of survival and detection processes. Some broods probably are much more likely to survive than others. Some broods probably are much more likely to be detected than others. So, I suspect the long-tailed exponential distribution is warranted, at least in theory. As a potential alternative to modeling random brood effects, I have also tinkered with analyzing bootstraps of data (encounter histories for one individual from each brood). I do not think this is a great solution in this system.

I am going to try a few more things and push ahead.

Thanks again.

Justin
